content.content:
# Measurement

Two things, both small: a weekly record of how Caliper compares with react-docgen-typescript (RDT) and react-docgen on five public repos, and `just bench` for a change that touches the resolver. Nothing here blocks a pull request.

## Weekly record

`.github/workflows/weekly.yml` runs on Mondays and by hand. `scripts/corpora.py` fetches each repo at a pinned commit and installs its dependencies with its own package manager and lockfile (lifecycle scripts off, caches under `.corpora/`, gitignored), then removes tests, stories, demos and `.d.ts` files from the source directory so every tool reads the same files. `scripts/weekly.py` runs the tools.

| Corpus | Repository | Commit | Source directory | Install |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| mantine | `mantinedev/mantine` | `e47e45af06427b3b2497100c2b849935c23af30d` | `packages/@mantine/core/src` | yarn, immutable |
| chakra | `chakra-ui/chakra-ui` | `fa9696f328ea5a0df8685c6d8460edbd779b63b9` | `packages/react/src` | pnpm, frozen |
| shadcn | `shadcn-ui/ui` | `ba1503c64472b82256d9de95e2e62c5901a38e8b` | `apps/v4` | pnpm, frozen |
| antd | `ant-design/ant-design` | `ba7ccbaa7b4b58ac1ff8e6fe2e78dfa10bfb5538` | `components` | npm, no lockfile (the repo commits none) |
| spectrum | `adobe/react-spectrum` | `797762ed3526ea12f089e321bd3891066affad70` | `packages` | yarn, immutable |

It records, per corpus and tool, the wall time and peak RSS of one whole run (process start and Node start included), and the size of Caliper's canonical JSON. Caliper runs with `--load-dependencies`; its time is the median of five runs. RDT and react-docgen run once each.

Each run's peak RSS is that process's own. `scripts/corpora.py` starts every measured command through a small helper that forks it and reads its `wait4` usage. Reading it straight from the weekly script gave one number for every run after the largest: on Linux a child's `ru_maxrss` starts at the highest RSS its parent ever had, and the script's own peak (it holds RDT's output for a large corpus) became every later tool's "peak". The first weekly record shows 1,593 MiB for all three tools on shadcn, antd and spectrum, which is that. `scripts/test_weekly.py` checks that a large parent no longer leaks in.

### The reference

Recall is measured against RDT's output, cleaned in two steps. Both are by what RDT reports, never by library or name lists, and `weekly.json` keeps their counts (`reference` per corpus) so a change in either is visible.

| Step | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Not components, left out | More than half of the props are declared in TypeScript's own `lib.*.d.ts` (the parameter is a `string`, a `Request`, a function: `GET`, `loadHighlighter`, `convertLegacyProps`). The name is a hook's (`use` and a capital). The only props are a `value` (and `children`) declared by `@types/react`, which is a context's Provider (`FormContext`). The name starts lowercase, is not the file's or directory's name (RDT names a default export after those) and no prop comes from `@types/react`, so it is no JSX tag and takes no tag's attributes (`genLinkStyle`, `generateMetadata`). Every prop is a `Promise<...>`, which a router hands over (`page`). |
| Repeats, counted once | RDT lists one component under each file that re-exports it, and names a default export after the file or directory (antd's `col/index.tsx` default-exports `Col` from `../grid` and RDT reports `col` there; Caliper reports the defining file). An entry that Caliper does not report in its own file pairs by evidence: where the default export, or the named export, of RDT's file is defined (followed through `export default X`, `import`, `export { X } from` and `export { default as X }`), or else the file that declares its props when Caliper reports a component of that name there. Entries that pair with the same Caliper component are one reference item. |

The record shows, per corpus: RDT's entries with props, how many are not components, how many repeats were merged, the reference size, how many match in the same file, how many are paired (by default export, named export or declaration) and how many stay unpaired. Pairing needs the names to agree: the component the export resolves to must have the name Caliper reports, so an entry never pairs with an unrelated component just because it is the only one in its file. When several RDT entries pair to one component, the reference takes the props of the entry in the component's own file, else the union of the repeats'. An unpaired item is a component Caliper does not report where RDT does, and it stays in the denominator.

The 2026-10-31 effect on the pinned corpora, Caliper's component recall (own and `@types/react` props are unchanged by the exclusions and move only a little with the pairing):

| Corpus | Reference before |                                           After | Components before | After |
| ------ | ---------------: | ----------------------------------------------: | ----------------: | ----: |
| shadcn |             1594 |                   1573 (21 left out, 0 repeats) |             95.2% | 96.5% |
| antd   |              258 | 203 (43 left out, 12 repeats merged, 12 paired) |             64.0% | 81.3% |

Exclusions alone give 76.7% on antd, pairing alone 68.3%. shadcn has no re-export of this kind in the pinned commit, so nothing pairs there; its unpaired items are `Icons.logo`-style object members, aliases such as `const ComboboxRoot = Primitive.Root` and factory results, which Caliper does not detect.

Recall is measured against that reference, on the components both tools report (same file, same name, or paired):

| Measure              | Meaning                                                                                   |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Components           | The reference's components that the tool also reports                                     |
| Own props            | Of those components, RDT's props not declared by `@types/react` that the tool lists       |
| `@types/react` props | RDT's props that `@types/react` declares (`onClick`, `aria-*`, `ref`) that the tool lists |
| ... with layers      | The same two, also counting a prop held in a collapsed inheritance layer                  |

Caliper collapses an inherited dependency source of more than 30 props into a layer (ADR 0012) and lists only its notable members as props, as Storybook does. A prop in a layer is in the output, named by the layer's `members`, but is not in the flat list, so the table reports both: the plain columns say what the default output lists, "with layers" says what it holds. react-docgen writes no layers, so its two columns are equal.

react-docgen reads each file alone with its default resolver and importer, as Storybook does, so it lists no types declared elsewhere. That is the point of the comparison.

The run uploads `weekly.json` and a table to the job summary. It compares with the last successful run's `weekly.json` and opens, or comments on, one issue labelled `weekly-measurement` when Caliper's time or memory is more than 10% worse, or its recall is more than 2 points lower, on any corpus. There is no committed baseline: the previous run is the baseline.

### TypeScript's checker as the oracle

RDT has mistakes of its own. With `--oracle` the run also asks TypeScript 7.1's checker (`apps/oracle/src/oracle.ts`, `typescript/sync` of `7.1.0-beta`) for each prop's type and compares it structurally with Caliper's canonical `--json`. The weekly table shows the share of props that agree (identical, or the same type spelled by name) and the share the checker contradicts. This is information only: the checker is a beta and the backend that uses it is an opt-in (`docs/type-checker-integration.md`).

| Verdict           | Meaning                                                                          |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Identical         | Both sides describe the same type                                                |
| Spelled           | The same type, Caliper by name where the checker expands it                      |
| Less precise      | Caliper's type is looser or left unevaluated                                     |
| Wrong             | Caliper's type describes something else, such as a literal union missing members |
| Checker any/error | The checker has no type                                                          |

## `just bench`

```bash
just bench                 # this checkout, uncommitted work included, against origin/main
just bench my-branch       # a branch
```

`scripts/bench.py` builds both in release mode, then times `extract --json` over Mantine and Chakra (source directory only, nothing installed, dependency loading off, no cache) with the two builds interleaved and alternating which goes first. It prints the median wall time and peak RSS of each and their ratio. The first run fetches the two source directories into `.corpora/`.

With nothing changed, the ratio stays inside 1.04 for time (95th percentile, 100 trials per corpus on CI and a laptop) and inside 1.12 for memory on CI runners. More than 1.10× in time or 1.20× in memory is worth looking at. Nothing enforces that. Run it before a resolver change goes up for review, and say in the pull request when a cost is intended.

## What this replaces

Before the weekly record, four workflows (Equivalence, Parity, Scorecard and Allow-list empty) ran against every pull request or `main` push, backed by `scripts/equivalence.py`, a per-pull-request allow-list directory and two committed baselines. They caught one regression in speed and one in output that review would have missed. They also failed on runner noise, on bases that had moved and on their own allow-list, and a lot of one week of merge work went to keeping them green. Git history has them.

What we give up: a pull request that slows the resolver or changes output no longer fails by itself. Review, `just bench` and the weekly issue catch it, the last one days later.

## Results, 2026-10-23

Measured with the parity script this replaces: `main` at `7bc120f4`, Apple Silicon laptop, 7 runs, with `--load-dependencies`.

| Corpus   | Components matched | Non-React props reported |           Caliper |               RDT |
| -------- | -----------------: | -----------------------: | ----------------: | ----------------: |
| mantine  |            331/389 |                    99.7% |    55 ms, 109 MiB |    1.3 s, 458 MiB |
| chakra   |            592/773 |                    98.6% | 550 ms, 1,461 MiB | 24.8 s, 1,550 MiB |
| shadcn   |          1519/1594 |                    39.5% |   115 ms, 181 MiB |  4.0 s, 1,149 MiB |
| antd     |            162/258 |                    80.3% |    86 ms, 127 MiB |  2.4 s, 1,033 MiB |

RDT's memory is its process's peak RSS and its time excludes Node's start; Caliper's time includes process start.
# Storybook parity

`packages/storybook/scripts/storybook-parity.mjs` measures the Storybook addon against Storybook's own docgen on real repositories: how often the addon hands a component on, what it documents that Storybook doesn't, where the two disagree, and what each costs. It is not run in CI; it needs the corpora `scripts/parity.py setup` fetches, installed, plus the native binding.

```bash
pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-storybook build
node packages/storybook/scripts/storybook-parity.mjs --corpora .corpora/repos --sample 120 --out report/storybook-parity
```

Output: `<out>.json` (every number) and `<out>.md` (tables). Storybook writes its cache into each corpus's `node_modules/.cache`, so the run needs write access there.

## What is compared

| Side | How it runs |
| --- | --- |
| Storybook's docgen | `@storybook/react`'s own `docgen-worker.js` (react-component-meta), unmodified, called as a middleware. It needs the TypeScript 5/6 compiler API, so `typescript` is redirected to `apps/oracle`'s TypeScript 6 (`--typescript` overrides); this package's TypeScript 7 has none. |
| The addon | `dist/provider.js`, the real `createDocgenProvider`, with Storybook's `meta.component` resolver and argTypes converter. |

Variants of the addon:

| Variant                | `loadDependencies` | `collapseInheritedProps` | `fallback`                           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| `caliper`              | on                 | none                     | degraded (the addon's defaults)      |
| `caliper-nodeps`       | off                | none                     | degraded (what the addon did before) |
| `caliper-curated`      | on                 | dependencies             | degraded                             |
| `caliper-never`        | on                 | none                     | never                                |
| `caliper-nodeps-never` | off                | none                     | never                                |

The `-never` variants answer for every component whatever its diagnostics say. Comparing them shows the information the addon holds; comparing the others shows what the `degraded` rule lets through.

Two story sets per corpus:

- **Real stories**: the corpus's own `*.stories.*` files that name `component:` (Chakra: 1 of 125, Spectrum: 129 of 132; Mantine, shadcn and antd have none).
- **Sampled components**: one generated `export default { component }` story per sampled component (`--sample`), written beside the component and removed afterwards. Components that aren't a named or default export are skipped.

Per story, both sides' argTypes are reduced to control kind (`type.name`), options, required, type text, default and whether a description exists, then diffed prop by prop. **Extra props** are props only the addon lists. The report also has the session-level fallback rate: components whose extraction carries a warning or error, over all components, without any story.

Not measured: Storybook's control inference from argTypes (kind is `type.name`), and runtime behaviour in a real Storybook process (the worker thread, concurrency, caching). Timings include the first request, which starts the session; the TypeScript baseline's include building its program. Storybook with thousands of stories scales differently from these samples.

## Results

2026-10-24, main through #152 plus the addon options of #155, Apple silicon. Peak RSS is the child process's.

### Fallback rate: components the addon would hand on

| Corpus   | Components | nodeps | deps (default) | deps, curated |
| -------- | ---------- | ------ | -------------- | ------------- |
| Mantine  | 344        | 70.1%  | 68.6%          | 68.6%         |
| Chakra   | 609        | 55.9%  | **92.1%**      | 92.1%         |
| shadcn   | 1892       | 45.8%  | 42.1%          | 40.6%         |
| antd     | 248        | 42.3%  | 27.4%          | 27.0%         |
| Spectrum | 1647       | 38.4%  | 37.9%          | 37.9%         |

Without them those components answer with almost no props (the 34 sampled Chakra stories it answers miss 39,008 props Storybook lists), so the `degraded` rule is right to hand them on.
- `collapseInheritedProps: 'dependencies'` changes nothing on Chakra, Mantine and Spectrum and trims shadcn (13,244 → 7,682 props).
- The leading reasons are unresolved references to dependency types (Chakra, Spectrum, antd), `cannot be used as a component` and `Cannot find the component whose props are referenced` (shadcn).

### Against Storybook's docgen (sampled components; `caliper` = the defaults)

| Corpus (stories) | Storybook s / MB | caliper s / MB, answered | caliper-never s / MB | Extra props | Props only Storybook lists | Default only Storybook |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mantine (18) | 1.0 / 462 | 0.2 / 252, 14 | 0.2 / 249 | 0 | 8 in 4 stories | 0 |
| Chakra (102) | 4.0 / 1186 | 0.8 / 787, **10** | 1.3 / 844 | 9 | 993 in 13 | 39 |
| shadcn (112) | 3.3 / 1218 | 0.8 / 323, 68 | 0.8 / 326 | 446 (87 described) | 76 in 21 | 21 |

| Spectrum real stories (129) | 1.3 / 686 | 2.8 / 340, 22 | 2.2 / 352 | 6530 (2390 described) | 0 | 0 |

- **Extra information.** What the addon lists and Storybook's docgen doesn't is inherited library props: DOM event handlers (`onPointerMoveCapture`), `aria-*`, Spectrum's style props (`UNSAFE_className`, `marginY`, `zIndex`), `isDisabled`/`isInvalid` from react-aria hooks. 38% of Spectrum's real-story extras and 20% of shadcn's carry a description. Whether that is more help or more noise in a controls panel is a product choice (`htmlAttributes`, `collapseInheritedProps`).
- **Cost.** The addon is 1.2–5× faster on these samples and uses 1.1–4× less memory (Chakra with dependencies is the exception: 844 MB against 1186 MB). The TypeScript baseline's time grows with the programs' size; the addon's first request pays the whole-corpus session.
- **Where the addon is behind.** Defaults Storybook reports and the addon doesn't (39–48 per corpus), 129 props in 13 antd stories, 993 in 13 Chakra stories, control kind differing on 60 of 917 shared antd props, and type text identical on only 60–70% of shared props (formatting included).
- **Reachability.** 20 antd and 114 of 129 real Spectrum stories name a component outside the configured `srcDirs` or a path the session can't match, which counts as handed on. Spectrum needed `starters` added to `srcDirs`.

The numbers to watch after the session work: the `caliper` degraded rate per corpus (target: below the `-never` gap), `Props only Storybook lists` (target 0), and the `caliper` seconds and MB columns for the first request.

content.content:
**Freshness.** tsc sees an edit to a dependency only when told:

```js
const s1 = await s0.update({ fileNotifications: { changed: [file] }, ensurePrograms: true })
```

With the notification, the dependent component's props updated (0.5 ms update, 2.8 ms query). An unnotified disk edit stayed stale (2026-09-20). Both incremental paths must notify it once the backend is wired in: `WatchSession::update_file` and `WatchSession::ensure_fresh`, which finds changes by stat instead of being told (ADR 0007 names only the first).

## Evidence

Method: RDT 2.4.0 on typescript@6.0.3 (`apps/oracle`'s RDT is pinned to a TS6 API — see "The RDT oracle" below) with the harness options (`shouldExtractLiteralValuesFromEnum`, `shouldRemoveUndefinedFromOptional`, `propFilter: { skipPropsWithoutDoc: false }`), against the algorithm above on the nightly named in each row, or `7.1.0-beta`. The harness that ran it (`apps/validate/src/run-semantic.ts` and `parity.ts`) was removed with the rest of the July fixtures harness: the table is the record, and re-running it means restoring those files from the repository history.

| Check | Result | Nightly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 13 components: the 10 outliers, base-ui `MenuRoot`, shadcn `Button`, mui `Button` | 0 missing and 0 extra props. `required` 3412/3412. Type strings 3410/3412 | 09-26 |
| Descriptions: ariakit, MUI, fluentui, shadcn | 294/294, 311/311, 288/288, 292/292 | 09-20 |
| `parent`: ariakit `MenuButton` | 294/294 in 12 requests | 09-20 |
| Fixture corpus, 55 files in one program | 70 components in common, equal prop counts on 70/70 | 09-20 |
| Class components | 2/2 on a synthetic file. The corpus has none | 09-20 |
| Full fixture corpus, 44 files / 47 components / 5554 props, one program | 5 missing, 27 extra. `required` 5508/5522. Type strings 5265/5522. Descriptions 47/47 | 09-26 |
| The same run | 5 missing, 27 extra. `required` 5508/5522. Type strings 5266/5522. Descriptions 47/47. Of the 13 components above, the two nested `ref` unions and ark-ui `SelectRoot.ids` differ | `7.1.0-beta` |

Type strings match after two normalizations. tsc prints union members in internal type-id order, which differs from TS 5.9, so members are compared as a set. RDT also runs `.replace(' | undefined', '')` twice, which turns a nested `=> string | undefined` into `=> string` and loses information. Canonical output keeps it. The 2 remaining differences are nested `ref` unions in fluentui and base-ui.

Of the corpus's 26 RDT-only entries, 23 have no props and 3 are default exports RDT names differently (mui `Button` confirmed at 311/311).

The full-corpus run's 257 remaining mismatches, unlike the curated 13, aren't all real algorithm gaps:

- Most are non-component exports the "single-parameter function" heuristic sweeps in — plain string-returning helpers (`antd/buttonHelpers.ts`, `headlessui/render.ts`'s `mergeProps`, `blueprint/blueprintTypes.ts`) whose "props" are `String.prototype`/`Array.prototype` members. RDT is equally permissive and picks these up too, so both tools agree these aren't components; the mismatches are TS 6 vs TS 7.1-dev lib.d.ts differences (e.g. `padStart`'s parameter renamed `maxLength`→`targetLength`) and per-run `Symbol.iterator` id suffixes, not a resolver bug.
- `children` without a description shows as "extra" — RDT drops it, canonical keeps it (see "What gets dropped", status Done).
- One real RDT bug surfaced: `rdt-compat/svg-icon.tsx` declares two `forwardRef` components (`Icon`, `Box`) in one file; RDT resolves `Box`'s `ref` and DOM-attribute types to `Icon`'s `SVGSVGElement` instead of `Box`'s own `HTMLDivElement`. The semantic algorithm gets `Box` right — RDT is the outlier.

## Cost

Measured through the Node client on one macOS machine, so a Rust client should be lower.

| Measure | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Spawn and first snapshot | 33–72 ms |
| First checker query | 1–15 ms |
| Request round trip | 0.1 ms. 500 positions in one request take about 1 ms |
| 55-file corpus, one program | 385 ms and 937 requests. RDT in-process: 955 ms |
| Server memory | About 100 MB (MUI `Button`) |
| Structural path, for comparison | 50 ms for the whole corpus, 1.75–2.1 ms per incremental update (`docs/benchmarks.md`) |

Trimming the process, on the MUI `Button` query (median of 5 runs, 2026-09-20). Differences under about 10 ms are noise.

| Config                                 |   Wall |    CPU | Memory |
| -------------------------------------- | -----: | -----: | -----: |
| Default                                |  85 ms | 270 ms | 102 MB |
| `types: []`                            |  79 ms | 260 ms | 100 MB |
| `types: []`, `GOGC=off`                |  71 ms | 200 ms | 111 MB |
| `types: []`, `GOMAXPROCS=2`            | 114 ms | 160 ms |  99 MB |
| Default, plus 300 unrelated root files |  88 ms | 320 ms | 112 MB |

Pass only the files you need as roots. The API's checker is lazy, and diagnostics and emit never run.

## Boundaries

- **`crates/core`** owns the semantic result type, the merge and the diagnostics. It has no I/O, no async and no protocol types. The merge lives here because `OpaqueDetail` and `ParsedProp` internals are `pub(crate)`.
- **Backend crate** (`crates/semantic`, always compiled in and enabled at run time, ADR 0007) spawns `tsc --api` through `crates/tsc-client`, runs the algorithm, and handles timeouts. Core never depends on it: the CLI runs the backend and calls core's `merge_semantic`.
- **CLI and NAPI** only switch it on. Neither calls JS.
- **Not a `DocgenPlugin`.** The hook is synchronous and runs on the cold path only. `WatchSession::update_file` skips plugins.
- **Failure** leaves the structural result and adds a diagnostic. It never fails extraction.
- **Determinism.** Reversing the query order changed no union order across 16 props in 3 files (2026-09-20). Whether canonical output sorts unions is open (below).

## Gates before it ships

| Gate | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Accuracy against RDT | Passed on 13 components and re-verified on the full 47-component fixture corpus. See Evidence and not verified below |
| Lifecycle | Client built and tested against a fake tsc and the real nightly (`crates/tsc-client`): missing binary, unsupported version, timeout, crash, restart storm, malformed or oversized frame, partial project failure, shutdown reaping, stale notification. Open: header-size cap, stderr that isn't UTF-8, honoring `handshake_timeout`, recovery after the restart cap trips, whether a restarted request may replay |
| Cost | Measured through the Node client. Repeat with the Rust client |
| Determinism | Clean and incremental runs must produce the same output |
| Oracle | Fixed. See below |

## The RDT oracle

`apps/oracle` depends on TypeScript 7.1 directly (for the oracle), but RDT 2.4.0 crashes on import against it (`ts.JsxEmit` is undefined). RDT now resolves its `typescript` peer to `typescript@6.0.3` instead, via the aliased `typescript-beta` dependency (`npm:typescript@7.1.0-beta`, pinned exactly) the oracle imports from — no pnpm override needed, since pnpm overrides don't reliably rewrite a peer dependency's resolution (tried `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s `overrides: { "react-docgen-typescript>typescript": ... }`; the lockfile recorded it but RDT kept resolving against whatever `typescript` apps/oracle depended on directly).

The removed harness's `compare.ts`/`analyze.ts` (caliper-docgen vs RDT/react-docgen) compared only name, `required`, type and default, and rendered our types themselves in `run-ours.ts` (objects print as `{ ... }`), so their type mismatches mixed resolver and renderer differences. Those limits went with it: `scripts/weekly.py` compares Caliper's own and `@types/react` props with RDT's by name, and the oracle compares prop types structurally against the TS 7.1 checker (`docs/measurement.md`).

## Open decisions

1. **Output type.** Checker types don't fit `PropType` losslessly: `Named` has no file or symbol, and `Tuple` has no optional or rest elements. Add a variant or map into existing ones. `ExtractionOutput` has no schema version, so add one first.
2. **`ref` and `key`.** RDT emits both, and nothing else records forwardRef metadata. Semantic mode must match whatever the structural path does.
3. **Trigger.** Run on every exported component or only on files with degrade diagnostics. Bare generic parameters and TypeScript utility types resolve to `Named` with no diagnostic by design, so the second misses them.
4. **Union order.** Sort in canonical output, or keep source order for structural results.

## Not verified

- Cost through the Rust client. Every measurement uses the Node client.
- Overloads with more than one signature, static sub-components (`Menu.Item`), and barrel re-exports, where RDT names components by the barrel file.
- `@default` and `@type` JSDoc overrides.
- Projects larger than the 44-file corpus.
- What the `MappedType` accessors added on 2026-09-23 ([#64397](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/pull/64397)) expose beyond resolved properties.
name: Weekly

# Caliper, react-docgen-typescript and react-docgen on five public repos with their dependencies installed: time,
# memory and recall (docs/measurement.md). It compares with last week's record and opens or updates one issue when
# Caliper got slower, bigger or less complete. It never runs on a pull request and never fails one.
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * 1"
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always
  CARGO_INCREMENTAL: "0"

jobs:
  weekly:
    name: Weekly
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 90
    permissions:
      contents: read
      actions: read
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - id: rust
        run: echo "version=$(sed -n 's/^rust = "\(.*\)"/\1/p' .prototools)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - uses: orin-dx/actions/setup-rust@2521888266780dabc7f5fd4c32b02d6ab82849db # v1.1
        with:
          toolchain: ${{ steps.rust.outputs.version }}
      # The corpora's own package managers run under Node 24: Yarn 4.18, which Mantine and React Spectrum pin, crashes
      # under the repository's Node 26 ("Dynamic require of "util" is not supported"). This step comes before the
      # toolchain's so that the toolchain's Node stays first on PATH for everything else; only the installs use this one.
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0

          node-version: "24"
          package-manager-cache: false
      - id: corpus-node
        run: echo "dir=$(dirname "$(command -v node)")" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      # RDT, react-docgen and the oracle run from apps/oracle's dependencies.
      - uses: moonrepo/setup-toolchain@261c62cb5b0f580c7be7c8cd0f023a2e96756095 # v0.6.4
        with:
          auto-install: true
      - uses: orin-dx/actions/setup-pnpm-cache@2521888266780dabc7f5fd4c32b02d6ab82849db # v1.1
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

        with:
          path: .corpora/caches
          key: weekly-${{ hashFiles('scripts/corpora.py', 'pnpm-lock.yaml') }}
      # A corpus that fails to install is named in the log with the tail of the install log; the others still install.
      - name: Fetch and install the corpora
        env:
          INSTALL_NODE_DIR: ${{ steps.corpus-node.outputs.dir }}
        run: python3 scripts/corpora.py setup --install-node-dir "$INSTALL_NODE_DIR"
      - name: Fetch last week's record
        continue-on-error: true
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          id=$(gh run list --workflow weekly.yml --status success --limit 1 --json databaseId --jq '.[0].databaseId // empty')
          if [ -n "$id" ]; then gh run download "$id" --name weekly --dir previous; fi
      - name: Measure
        run: >-
          python3 scripts/weekly.py --bin target/release/caliper-docgen --oracle --previous previous/weekly.json
          --out weekly.json --markdown weekly.md --issue issue.md

        run: cat weekly.md >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY" || true

            .corpora/logs

        if: ${{ hashFiles('issue.md') != '' }}
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          gh label create weekly-measurement --description "Caliper got worse in the weekly record" --color D93F0B 2>/dev/null || true
          existing=$(gh issue list --label weekly-measurement --state open --json number --jq '.[0].number // empty')
          if [ -n "$existing" ]; then
            gh issue comment "$existing" --body-file issue.md
          else
            gh issue create --title "The weekly record got worse" --label weekly-measurement --body-file issue.md
          fi
// The oracle's comparison is pure, so its verdicts are tested without a checker.
import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest'
import { compare, prim, type Norm } from '../src/oracle-compare.ts'

const lit = (value: string): Norm => ({ k: 'lit', value })
const union = (...members: Norm[]): Norm => ({ k: 'union', members })
const undef = prim('undefined')
const optional = (type: Norm): Norm => union(type, undef)

describe('the oracle comparison', () => {
  it('a type parameter Caliper replaced with its default is one instance of it, not another type', () => {
    expect.hasAssertions()
    // `multiple?: Multiple` with `Multiple extends boolean = false`, which Caliper reads as `false`.
    const multiple: Norm = { k: 'param', name: 'Multiple', fallback: lit('false'), constraint: prim('boolean') }
    expect(compare(lit('false'), optional(multiple))).toBe('less precise')
    expect(compare(prim('boolean'), optional(multiple))).toBe('less precise')
  })

  it('a parameter with neither a default nor a constraint holds whatever instance Caliper picked', () => {
    expect.hasAssertions()
    // antd's `Segmented`: `defaultValue?: ValueType` where the cast over `forwardRef` declares `<ValueType>` bare and
    // the props interface declares the default Caliper used.
    const valueType: Norm = { k: 'param', name: 'ValueType' }
    expect(compare(union(prim('string'), prim('number')), optional(valueType))).toBe('less precise')
  })

  it('a literal a primitive of its kind in the same union covers adds nothing', () => {
    expect.hasAssertions()
    // antd's `DrawerPanel`: `size?: 'default' | 'large' | number | string`, which the checker reduces to `string | number`.
    const written = union(lit('default'), lit('large'), prim('number'), prim('string'))
    expect(compare(written, optional(union(prim('string'), prim('number'))))).toBe('identical')
    // Without the primitive the literals are still the type.
    expect(compare(union(lit('default'), lit('large')), optional(union(lit('default'), lit('large'))))).toBe(
      'identical',
    )
    // A numeric literal is covered by `number`, not by `string`.
    expect(compare(union(lit('1'), prim('string')), optional(union(lit('1'), prim('string'))))).toBe('identical')
  })

  it('a type parameter replaced with its constraint is one instance of it', () => {
    expect.hasAssertions()
    // `value?: Value` with `Value extends string`, which Caliper reads as `string`.
    const value: Norm = { k: 'param', name: 'Value', constraint: prim('string') }
    expect(compare(prim('string'), optional(value))).toBe('less precise')
  })

  it('a type that is neither the default nor the constraint of the parameter is wrong', () => {
    expect.hasAssertions()
    const value: Norm = { k: 'param', name: 'Value', fallback: prim('string'), constraint: prim('string') }
    expect(compare(prim('number'), optional(value))).toBe('wrong')
  })

  it('a union Caliper wrote out fits a parameter whose default is that union', () => {
    expect.hasAssertions()
    // `value?: ValueType` with `ValueType extends SegmentedValue = SegmentedValue`, and `SegmentedValue = string | number`.
    const both = union(prim('string'), prim('number'))
    const valueType: Norm = { k: 'param', name: 'ValueType', fallback: both, constraint: both }
    expect(compare(both, optional(valueType))).toBe('less precise')
    expect(compare(union(prim('string'), prim('boolean')), optional(valueType))).toBe('wrong')
  })

  it('a type parameter inside an array is compared through the same instances', () => {
    expect.hasAssertions()
    const value: Norm = { k: 'param', name: 'Value', constraint: prim('string') }
    const checker: Norm = { k: 'array', element: value }
    expect(compare({ k: 'array', element: prim('string') }, checker)).toBe('less precise')
    expect(compare({ k: 'array', element: prim('number') }, checker)).toBe('wrong')
  })

  it('an optional prop of type never is undefined in the checker', () => {
    expect.hasAssertions()
    // `classNames?: never` reads `undefined`, the optional marker the comparison drops.
    expect(compare(prim('never'), undef)).toBe('identical')
    expect(compare(prim('never'), prim('string'))).toBe('wrong')
    expect(compare(prim('string'), undef)).toBe('wrong')
  })
})

input.topic: Fair three-way (Caliper, RDT, vanilla react-docgen) comparison against the TS 7.1 checker oracle
input.headline: The oracle's pure compare() already scores any tool that can be reduced to its Norm shape. I prototyped both adapters (RDT type strings, react-docgen tsType.raw) in an uncommitted scratch file and ran them through the unchanged compare() on three fixtures (27 props). Verdicts came out sensible, and the prototype is deleted. Four things need fixing first. rdt.mjs stores only the string "enum" for enum props (4 to 5% of own props). weekly.py's react-docgen run uses the default resolver and loses 17 to 21% of files to thrown errors (the failed count is not recorded). compareFunctions caps any optional or rest parameter at 'less precise' for every tool. The vanilla react-docgen wording in the docs is partly wrong (it follows relative imports). Cost is small: the program and compare passes are already paid, and extra tools add only string parsing, deduped per distinct string.

findings.claim: oracle.ts verdict rules for Caliper: caliperNorm (oracle-compare.ts:43-80) maps canonical PropType to Norm. Depth over MAX_DEPTH=3 gives opaque; 'named' gives name; a known terminal gives name; any other kind gives opaque. compare() (198-233) applies these rules in order. (1) checker error/any, or top-level unknown, gives 'checker any/error' at depth 0 and 'identical' deeper. (2) Caliper name: 'spelled' if the checker alias or declaring symbol name matches, 'identical' if it names the same type parameter, otherwise 'less precise' (never 'wrong'). (3) checker opaque gives identical; Caliper opaque gives 'less precise'. (4) Caliper any/unknown against another type gives 'less precise'. (5) An unreduced intersection gives 'less precise'. (6) members() drops undefined, folds true|false to boolean, and drops literals covered by a same-kind primitive on the written side only. Two or more members go to compareUnions: each checker member must be covered, and each Caliper member matched; a wide primitive against literals is 'less precise'. (7) compareOne per kind: prim and lit mismatch gives wrong; lit against string/number/boolean gives less precise; tuple against array gives less precise; object fields not in the checker give wrong, missing fields or an index give less precise; function params are compared one by one; param is 'less precise' if it fits the default or constraint, else wrong.
findings.evidence: apps/oracle/src/oracle-compare.ts:43-233; oracle-checker.ts:36-150 (typeName 25-33, union alias recovery 91-100); VERIFIED by reading. Aggregates: oracle.ts:325-326 agree=(identical+spelled)/shared, wrong=wrong/shared.

findings.claim: Universe and matching today: components are the checker's exported call/construct signatures with one parameter or one named props (oracle.ts:93-106), matched to Caliper by file and normalized name (201-206); a name matching more than one Caliper component is skipped as ambiguous. Props that are ref, key or declared under /@types/react/ are excluded (194-199). Shared props are scored. Absent props are 'missing', or 'collapsed' when declared in an inheritance layer of more than 30 props (210-221). Verdicts are cached per (Caliper prop id, checker type id).
findings.evidence: apps/oracle/src/oracle.ts:93-262 (read). Weekly 41479003541 log: mantine 334/370 components, 20,104 shared props; chakra 620/790, 486,752; shadcn 1538/1580, 7,632; antd 187/310, 3,070; spectrum 512/1365, 2,023.

findings.claim: A function type with an optional or rest parameter can never score better than 'less precise' for ANY tool, even one that preserved the marker. compareFunctions (oracle-compare.ts:141) pushes 'less precise' whenever the checker param is optional or rest, regardless of what the tool wrote. Caliper records neither marker (line 70), so its numbers do not change if the rule becomes (kp.optional && !cp.optional) || (kp.rest && !cp.rest).
findings.evidence: Scratch run on `fn?: (a?: string, ...rest: number[]) => Promise<void>`: Caliper, RDT and react-docgen all returned 'less precise', though RDT and react-docgen texts carry both markers and my adapters parsed them (the oracle's checker side also reported them).

findings.claim: RDT output shape per prop (2.4.0, harness options): type {name, raw?, value?}, required, defaultValue ({value} or null), description, parent {fileName,name}, declarations [{fileName,name}]. Enum shapes: a type whose members are all literals gives name:'enum' with raw (the written text, or an alias name like 'Tone' or 'Mode') and value:[{value:'"sm"'},...]. A union containing null is NOT an enum (name is a plain string such as '"default" | ... | null' with no raw). Aliases of non-literal types print by name ('Remote', 'Pair', 'Item<number>[]', 'CSSProperties', 'MouseEventHandler<HTMLSpanElement>'). Type parameters erase to the constraint (`gen?: T` prints 'string'). Function types print parenthesised and keep '?' and '...'. Undocumented `children` is dropped (13 Caliper props, 12 RDT). A prop with no declaration (VariantProps in shadcn Badge) has parent undefined.
findings.evidence: Ran node with react-docgen-typescript on a 13-prop fixture, an inherited-props fixture, a shapes fixture, and shadcn registry/new-york-v4/ui/badge.tsx (variant: name '"default" | "secondary" | ... | null', defaultValue {value:'default'}, declarations []; asChild declared in TypeLiteral).

findings.claim: scripts/rdt.mjs:31 writes `type: p.type?.name`, so every enum prop becomes the bare string 'enum' and loses raw and value. Survey of the existing RDT dumps, own props only (react-declared excluded): shadcn 581 of 14,492 (4.0%), antd 320 of 5,966 (5.4%). An RDT adapter needs the whole type object. Also dump only own props (not parent under @types/react) so chakra's ~490k props stay small.

Verdicts came out sensible, and the prototype is deleted. findings.claim: oracle.ts verdict rules for Caliper: caliperNorm (oracle-compare.ts:43-80) maps canonical PropType to Norm. Depth over MAX_DEPTH=3 gives opaque; 'named' gives name; a known terminal gives name; any other kind gives opaque. compare() (198-233) applies these rules in order. (1) checker error/any, or top-level unknown, gives 'checker any/error' at depth 0 and 'identical' deeper. (2) Caliper name: 'spelled' if the checker alias or declaring symbol name matches, 'identical' if it names the same type parameter, otherwise 'less precise' (never 'wrong'). (3) checker opaque gives identical; Caliper opaque gives 'less precise'. (4) Caliper any/unknown against another type gives 'less precise'. (5) An unreduced intersection gives 'less precise'. (6) members() drops undefined, folds true|false to boolean, and drops literals covered by a same-kind primitive on the written side only. Two or more members go to compareUnions: each checker member must be covered, and each Caliper member matched; a wide primitive against literals is 'less precise'. (7) compareOne per kind: prim and lit mismatch gives wrong; lit against string/number/boolean gives less precise; tuple against array gives less precise; object fields not in the checker give wrong, missing fields or an index give less precise; function params are compared one by one; param is 'less precise' if it fits the default or constraint, else wrong.

Results (cal / rdt / rdg): label identical x3; size identical, identical, less precise (typeof SIZES[number] is opaque); tone ident x3; mode spelled / identical (enum values) / spelled; remote identical / spelled / identical; style, onChange, list, as, rec: spelled x3; gen (type param T) identical / less precise (RDT prints 'string') / identical; ro (readonly string[]) less precise / identical / less precise; keyed (keyof) less precise x3 (rdg is actually wrong, hidden by the name rule); tuple identical / spelled / identical; children spelled / no-prop (RDT drops) / spelled; fn less precise x3 (the optional-param rule above).

findings.claim: Name rule gap that matters for a fair comparison: compareOne never returns 'wrong' for a printed name (oracle-compare.ts:210-220), so a wrong named type (react-docgen's 'Opt' for keyof Opt) scores 'less precise', not 'wrong'. The 'wrong' column therefore understates errors for tools that print names (RDT, react-docgen, Caliper named). Also 'spelled' (a name the checker aliases) is not worse than 'identical' for a reader, but identical-vs-spelled splits tools by style: RDT mostly prints alias names, Caliper and react-docgen expand more. The headline must be agree=(identical+spelled), with identical and spelled reported separately. Args on generics are ignored by every tool (Item<number> and Item<string> both match).

findings.claim: Facts scoreable against the checker. required: yes, the symbol is not SymbolFlags.Optional (oracle-checker.ts:126 already uses Optional for parameters); `required: number | undefined` is required in all three tools. findings.claim: Prop universe design. Universe = checker own props of each checker-found component (oracle.ts rules: not ref, key, or @types/react). Key = (file, normalized component name, prop). Caliper's 'collapsed' layer props count as listed-in-layer, as in the existing rule. Headline per tool: agree divided by the universe (unconditional) alongside listed/universe and agree among listed; conditional rates alone are not comparable because the listed sets differ.

data.topic: Fair three-way (Caliper, RDT, vanilla react-docgen) comparison against the TS 7.1 checker oracle
data.headline: The oracle's pure compare() already scores any tool that can be reduced to its Norm shape. I prototyped both adapters (RDT type strings, react-docgen tsType.raw) in an uncommitted scratch file and ran them through the unchanged compare() on three fixtures (27 props). Verdicts came out sensible, and the prototype is deleted. Four things need fixing first. rdt.mjs stores only the string "enum" for enum props (4 to 5% of own props). weekly.py's react-docgen run uses the default resolver and loses 17 to 21% of files to thrown errors (the failed count is not recorded). compareFunctions caps any optional or rest parameter at 'less precise' for every tool. The vanilla react-docgen wording in the docs is partly wrong (it follows relative imports). Cost is small: the program and compare passes are already paid, and extra tools add only string parsing, deduped per distinct string.

findings.claim: oracle.ts verdict rules for Caliper: caliperNorm (oracle-compare.ts:43-80) maps canonical PropType to Norm. Depth over MAX_DEPTH=3 gives opaque; 'named' gives name; a known terminal gives name; any other kind gives opaque. compare() (198-233) applies these rules in order. (1) checker error/any, or top-level unknown, gives 'checker any/error' at depth 0 and 'identical' deeper. (2) Caliper name: 'spelled' if the checker alias or declaring symbol name matches, 'identical' if it names the same type parameter, otherwise 'less precise' (never 'wrong'). (3) checker opaque gives identical; Caliper opaque gives 'less precise'. (4) Caliper any/unknown against another type gives 'less precise'. (5) An unreduced intersection gives 'less precise'. (6) members() drops undefined, folds true|false to boolean, and drops literals covered by a same-kind primitive on the written side only. Two or more members go to compareUnions: each checker member must be covered, and each Caliper member matched; a wide primitive against literals is 'less precise'. (7) compareOne per kind: prim and lit mismatch gives wrong; lit against string/number/boolean gives less precise; tuple against array gives less precise; object fields not in the checker give wrong, missing fields or an index give less precise; function params are compared one by one; param is 'less precise' if it fits the default or constraint, else wrong.
findings.evidence: apps/oracle/src/oracle-compare.ts:43-233; oracle-checker.ts:36-150 (typeName 25-33, union alias recovery 91-100); VERIFIED by reading. Aggregates: oracle.ts:325-326 agree=(identical+spelled)/shared, wrong=wrong/shared.

findings.claim: Universe and matching today: components are the checker's exported call/construct signatures with one parameter or one named props (oracle.ts:93-106), matched to Caliper by file and normalized name (201-206); a name matching more than one Caliper component is skipped as ambiguous. Props that are ref, key or declared under /@types/react/ are excluded (194-199). Shared props are scored. Absent props are 'missing', or 'collapsed' when declared in an inheritance layer of more than 30 props (210-221). Verdicts are cached per (Caliper prop id, checker type id).

findings.claim: A function type with an optional or rest parameter can never score better than 'less precise' for ANY tool, even one that preserved the marker. compareFunctions (oracle-compare.ts:141) pushes 'less precise' whenever the checker param is optional or rest, regardless of what the tool wrote. Caliper records neither marker (line 70), so its numbers do not change if the rule becomes (kp.optional && !cp.optional) || (kp.rest && !cp.rest).

findings.claim: RDT output shape per prop (2.4.0, harness options): type {name, raw?, value?}, required, defaultValue ({value} or null), description, parent {fileName,name}, declarations [{fileName,name}]. Enum shapes: a type whose members are all literals gives name:'enum' with raw (the written text, or an alias name like 'Tone' or 'Mode') and value:[{value:'"sm"'},...]. A union containing null is NOT an enum (name is a plain string such as '"default" | ... | null' with no raw). Aliases of non-literal types print by name ('Remote', 'Pair', 'Item<number>[]', 'CSSProperties', 'MouseEventHandler<HTMLSpanElement>'). Type parameters erase to the constraint (`gen?: T` prints 'string'). Function types print parenthesised and keep '?' and '...'. Undocumented `children` is dropped (13 Caliper props, 12 RDT). A prop with no declaration (VariantProps in shadcn Badge) has parent undefined.

findings.claim: scripts/rdt.mjs:31 writes `type: p.type?.name`, so every enum prop becomes the bare string 'enum' and loses raw and value. Survey of the existing RDT dumps, own props only (react-declared excluded): shadcn 581 of 14,492 (4.0%), antd 320 of 5,966 (5.4%). An RDT adapter needs the whole type object. Also dump only own props (not parent under @types/react) so chakra's ~490k props stay small.

findings.claim: react-docgen 8.0.4 shape per prop: tsType {name, raw?, elements?, signature?}, required, defaultValue {value (source text, e.g. "'md'"), computed}, description (JSDoc; tags such as @default folded into the text). Unions give name:'union', elements of {name:'literal', value:"'info'"}, plus raw. Arrays give name:'Array', elements, raw 'string[]'. Functions give name:'signature', type:'function', signature.arguments [{name,type,rest?}] and return; optional-parameter flags are NOT recorded, so use raw. Objects give signature.type 'object' with properties [{key,value:{name,required}}]. Namespaced names are mangled ('ReactRef', raw 'React.Ref<...>'). A local alias is expanded to its text (Tone to a union of literals) but TS enums stay named ('Mode'). A typeof or indexed type gives name 'unknown[number]'. Failures: `ro?: readonly string[]` gives name 'unknown'; optional tuple element gives 'unknown'; and `keyed?: keyof Opt` gives name 'Opt', which is WRONG (the checker has keyof Opt = string|number|... ). A prop whose type is unresolvable (VariantProps<...>) has no tsType at all; its defaultValue is still present.
findings.evidence: Ran react-docgen 8.0.4 parse() on the three fixtures and on shadcn badge.tsx (variant: no tsType, defaultValue "default"; asChild: boolean). Wrong keyof result seen in the Shapes fixture output.

findings.claim: Vanilla react-docgen is not 'a file alone with no knowledge of other files' as scripts/rdg.mjs:3-4 and docs/measurement.md say. The default importer is fsImporter (node `resolve`, dist/main.js comment). It followed a relative `import type { Remote } from './remote'` and `extends BaseProps from './base'` (base prop with its JSDoc was listed). It did NOT list any @types/react prop (Imp: 2 props vs RDT 289 and Caliper 290), because `React.ButtonHTMLAttributes` is a namespace member. Whether it resolves other node_modules package sources was not tested.

findings.claim: weekly's react-docgen run uses the default resolver, which accepts one exported component per file and throws on more. On the corpora: shadcn 265 of 1,240 files fail (208 MULTIPLE_DEFINITIONS, 57 MISSING_DEFINITION), 975 components; antd 51 of 295 fail (14 and 37), 244 components. With FindExportedDefinitionsResolver({limit:0}) the same files give 2,332 components in shadcn (208 more files parse) and 274 in antd. weekly.json does not record `failed` (tool_run keeps only ms and rss). Caliper's 'collapsed' layer props count as listed-in-layer, as in the existing rule. Headline per tool: agree divided by the universe (unconditional) alongside listed/universe and agree among listed; conditional rates alone are not comparable because the listed sets differ.

proposed_branches.name: oracle/function-marker-rule
proposed_branches.scope: Fix compareFunctions so an optional or rest checker parameter is 'less precise' only if the tool did not record it: (kp.optional && !cp.optional) || (kp.rest && !cp.rest). Caliper records neither marker, so its numbers must not change. Add pure tests.
proposed_branches.tests: Pure: function with optional param, tool has marker gives identical; tool lacks it gives 'less precise'; rest likewise; an extra tool param stays 'wrong'. Verify a weekly --oracle run on antd and shadcn leaves Caliper's agree and wrong equal.
proposed_branches.cost_note: No runtime cost. Paid once per distinct comparison, which is already cached.
proposed_branches.expected_gain: Removes a bias against tools that keep markers; Caliper's own numbers unchanged.

proposed_branches.name: oracle/tool-adapters
proposed_branches.scope: New pure module apps/oracle/src/tool-norm.ts: rdtNorm(typeObject) (enum value[] gives literal union, else parse name) and rdgNorm(tsType) (parse raw ?? name, no tsType gives 'no type'), both through one TS-string to Norm mapper (KeywordType, LiteralType, Union, Intersection, Array/Array<T>/readonly, Tuple, FunctionType and single-call TypeLiteral, TypeLiteral fields and index, TypeReference to name via bareName, anything else opaque; a parse error or '...' truncation gives opaque, not error). Cache per distinct string. Also change scripts/rdt.mjs to keep the full type object for own props and drop @types/react props and declarations; scripts/rdg.mjs to keep tsType and record the failed count (and the resolver in use).
proposed_branches.tests: Pure unit tests with exact Norm expectations plus compare() verdicts against hand-built checker Norms. RDT: {name:'enum',raw:'Tone',value:["'info'","'warn'"]} to union of lits; 'string | null'; '((a?: string, ...rest: number[]) => Promise<void>)' to function with optional and rest markers; 'Item<number>[]' to array of name Item; 'string' for a type param T gives 'less precise' against param T. react-docgen: raw "'info' | 'warn'", Array raw 'string[]', mangled 'ReactCSSProperties' with raw 'React.CSSProperties' to name CSSProperties, name 'unknown[number]' to opaque, missing tsType to 'no type'. Integration fixture with the 27-prop table in the findings as exact expected verdicts per tool (run live; needs typescript-beta).
proposed_branches.cost_note: Per distinct type string: one TS parse (cached). Per prop: a map lookup. No per-run cost beyond reading the two dumps.
proposed_branches.expected_gain: RDT and react-docgen scorable by the same rules; no change to Caliper's numbers.

proposed_branches.name: oracle/three-tools-report
proposed_branches.scope: oracle.ts takes optional --rdt and --rdg dump files and computes per tool: component found/errored/absent, universe, listed, missing by declaration stratum, extra, verdict counts including 'no type' and 'unparsed', and required, enum-option agreement. weekly.py oracle() passes the dumps, and the result is nested: entry['oracle'] keeps shared_props/agree/wrong for Caliper (continuity) and adds 'tools' {caliper, rdt, react_docgen} with the fields above plus program_ms, compare_ms. markdown() gets a per-corpus x tool table: Universe, Listed, Agree of universe, Agree of listed, Identical, Spelled, Less precise, Wrong, No type, Required match, Options match, plus a missing-by-stratum table (same file, other file, dependency). findings() unchanged: still never a gate. Weekly run uses react-docgen's component errors and lists them.
proposed_branches.tests: test_weekly.py: markdown with a three-tool oracle block and with an old single-tool block (previous records); oracle() result shape. The vitest fixture from the adapters branch asserts the counts. One real weekly run on shadcn and antd with the work dir to compare before/after for Caliper's agree/wrong.
proposed_branches.cost_note: Per run: about +5 to 15 s on the weekly Measure step (inferred); chakra is the only corpus where per-prop work (487k lookups per tool) is noticeable. Per component: one extra Map lookup.
proposed_branches.expected_gain: The weekly record shows all three tools against the same oracle.

proposed_branches.name: oracle/default-and-description
proposed_branches.scope: Optional second step: score default values against a TS 6 syntactic oracle (destructuring initializers, @default), and descriptions as three-way agreement (not checker truth). Report separately and label each as not independent from RDT.
proposed_branches.tests: Fixture defaults: size = 'md' destructured; @default 'md' tag; disabled = false; a defaultProps case. Expected per tool match or miss in a table.
proposed_branches.cost_note: One extra TS 6 program per corpus (per run); cost not measured. The 7.1 sync API has no JSDoc accessor.
proposed_branches.expected_gain: Covers the facts the checker cannot judge; lower confidence than types.

risks: rdt.mjs and rdg.mjs output formats change, and test_weekly.py or other readers of weekly components break; keep the old fields and add new ones.
Chakra's RDT dump is large; the existing 8 GB Node heap and 2 GiB RSS may grow if declarations and react props are kept. Filter in rdt.mjs.
Choice of react-docgen resolver can swing component recall from 975 to 2,332 components on shadcn; reporting only one may be read as a Caliper-friendly or hostile choice.
'Less precise' for any printed name that does not match an alias hides wrong names (react-docgen keyof Opt gives Opt); adding a 'wrong' rule changes Caliper's historical numbers.
The 7.1 checker is a beta and a 'wrong' from the oracle can be the oracle's own mistake (spectrum 1.09% wrong; Chakra had one wrong in 487k).

The oracle universe drops @types/react props, so the three-way table says nothing about the React-attribute props where RDT and Caliper outperform vanilla react-docgen by construction; keep the existing recall table beside it.
RDT, like the oracle, relies on the TS compiler; scoring its descriptions and defaults against TS 6 facts is circular.
open_questions_for_user: Which react-docgen resolver is 'vanilla'? The current default (one component per file, throws on the rest: 21% of shadcn files) or an all-exported resolver (2,332 components)? Storybook's actual plugin configuration was not verified here. Preferred: report both, labelled, or verify Storybook's setup first.
Is the headline 'agree of universe' (unconditional), with 'agree of listed' secondary? Otherwise the per-tool rates are not comparable.

May compareFunctions and the name rule change? Function markers change nothing for Caliper; a 'wrong' for mismatched names would shift Caliper's historical numbers (decide: new column 'name mismatch' or retro-compare).
Should the report stratify missing props by where the checker says they are declared (same file, other file, dependency) and show that stratum for vanilla react-docgen? Recommended.
Include react-docgen's thrown files as a component-level miss or exclude them from the universe? Recommended: count them, shown as their own column.
Are default values and descriptions in scope for the first PR or a follow-up? The checker cannot judge either, and RDT shares the TS 6 engine.

How should RDT's undocumented-children drop and the string-lib noise entries (components whose props are String.prototype members) be handled? Reuse weekly.py exclusion() for the component universe, or follow the oracle's checker-first discovery?
